## Prerequisites & Learning Objectives

### Prerequisites

Before studying this chapter, make sure you are comfortable with:

- **Chapter 05 & Chapter 08 (Bipartite Matching & DAG Path Covers)**: Splitting each vertex $v \in V$ of a directed graph into an outgoing port $v_{\text{out}}$ and an incoming port $v_{\text{in}}$ so that an unweighted matching of size $M$ partitions a DAG into $N - M$ vertex-disjoint directed paths.
- **Chapter 17 (Min-Cost Max-Flow Foundations & Potentials)**: Running the Successive Shortest Path (SSP) algorithm with Johnson potentials $\pi_v$ ($\tilde{c}(u, v) = c(u, v) + \pi_u - \pi_v \ge 0$), initializing potentials via topological DP on DAGs, and reversing saturated forward arcs $(u, v)$ into backward residual arcs $(v, u)$ of cost $-c(u, v)$.
- **Chapter 18 & Chapter 19 (Convex Marginal Arcs & Equation-Difference Compilation)**: Encoding discrete convex functions via parallel unit-capacity arcs of non-decreasing marginal cost $\Delta g(k) = g(k) - g(k-1)$, and compiling flow balance equations via demand substitution $f(e) = L(e) + y_e$ or consecutive equation differencing $\Delta E_t = E_t - E_{t-1}$.

### Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. **Apply the Unifying Spine of Bipartite Supply–Demand Splitting (`拆点供需`) and Transition Kernel Factorization**: Recognize when an entity simultaneously acts as a producer of outgoing state and a consumer of incoming state, decouple it into $(i_{\text{out}} \in \mathcal{S}, i_{\text{in}} \in \mathcal{D})$, and factor dense $O(N^2)$ transition kernels $K(i, j) = \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\big(\alpha(i, h) + \beta(h, j)\big)$ through compact intermediate hub layers $\mathcal{H}$.
2. **Compile Min-Cost Cycle Covers and Precedence-Locked Path Covers**: Model degree-$1$ cycle covers on toroidal grids (**[TJOI2013] Cyclic Grid `循环格`, `#153`**), convert cycle covers into $K$-path covers via reset/starter hubs $H_{\text{start}}$, and precompute restricted Floyd–Warshall metric closures $d^{(\le \max(u,v))}(u, v)$ when vertices must be unlocked in strict index order (**[ZJOI2011] Rescuing Pikachu `营救皮卡丘`, `#157`**).
3. **Decouple Time-Delayed Resource Refurbishment and $K$-Slot Caching**: Prove why a single vertex per day fails (**Failure Mode `FM-20a`**) in **[Luogu P1251] Napkin Plan (`餐巾计划问题`, `#155`)**, derive the exact algebraic equivalence between lower-bound demand substitution and the Bipartite Dirty/Clean Split $(d_t \in \mathcal{S}, c_t \in \mathcal{D})$, and compile offline weighted caching (**Codeforces 802 C — Heidi and Library, `#158`**).
4. **Master Reverse Queue-Position Factorization and Dynamic Lazy Node Spawning (`动态加点`)**: Transform the total waiting time on heterogeneous parallel machines into $\sum_{r=1}^k r \cdot t_{k-r+1}$ where $r$ indexes slots **backward from the end of each chef's queue** (**[SCOI2007] Car Repair `修车`, `#154`**; **Failure Mode `FM-20b`**), prove the **Frontier Slot Dominance Theorem**, and shrink $3.2 \times 10^6$ static edges to $\le 36,000$ active edges via on-demand lazy vertex spawning (**[NOI2012] Food Festival `美食节`, `#156`**).
5. **Construct Non-Graph Order-Statistic Rank Hubs and 4-Sign Manhattan Hubs**: Solve **[AtCoder AGC 031 E — Snuke the Phantom Thief](https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc031/tasks/agc031_e) (`#159`)** by translating 2D half-plane count constraints into monotone rank-slot intervals $[L_r, R_r] \times [D_r, U_r]$ proved exact by the **Monotone Interval Uncrossing Theorem**, and solve **[AtCoder AGC 034 D — Manhattan Max Matching](https://atcoder.jp/contests/agc034/tasks/agc034_d) (`#160`)** in $O(N \log N)$ per augmentation by factoring $|x_i - x_j| + |y_i - y_j|$ through $2^2 = 4$ global sign hubs $H_{\pm, \pm}$.

## 1. Unifying Spine: Bipartite Supply–Demand Splitting (`拆点供需`) & Transition Kernel Factorization

### 1.1 The Two Structural Bottlenecks of Multi-Agent, Dynamic, and Geometric MCMF

In Chapters 17 through 19, the flow conservation structure was visible on a single timeline or graph: a token entered at $S$, moved chronologically from $t$ to $t+1$ (or hopped across an interval chord $l_i \to r_i + 1$), and exited at $T$. As we move into upper-division olympiad and Grandmaster contest problems, two fundamental modelling barriers appear:

1. **The Coupled-Role Self-Loop Barrier (Why Single-Vertex Conservation Short-Circuits)**:
   In many problems, each entity $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ must *both* **satisfy a mandatory incoming demand** and **generate an outgoing supply** that transitions to a different entity $j$:
   - On a directed graph or torus grid, every cell $i$ must be **entered** exactly once (`in-degree = 1`) and **exited** exactly once (`out-degree = 1`).
   - In a daily napkin laundering schedule, day $t$ must **consume** $r_t$ clean napkins in the morning and **release** $r_t$ dirty napkins in the evening.
   - In a $K$-slot library cache, request $t$ must **receive** book $a_t$ in an active cache slot and then **release** that cache slot to either hold $a_t$ until its next request $t'$ or fetch a different book.
   If we represent entity $i$ by a single flow vertex, any supply injected into $i$ immediately exits through $i$'s own demand arc to $T$ at cost $0$—short-circuiting the actual transition between $i$ and $j$!

2. **The Dense / Non-Linear Transition Kernel Barrier ($O(N^2)$ or $O(N^2 M)$ Edge Explosion)**:
   Even after splitting entities into supply and demand ports, connecting every supply port $i_{\text{out}} \in \mathcal{S}$ directly to every compatible demand port $j_{\text{in}} \in \mathcal{D}$ with transition cost $K(i, j)$ often either:
   - Depends on **how many other items** are assigned to the same machine (in parallel machine scheduling, where a job's delay depends on the queue behind it),
   - Couples 2D prefix/suffix counts across all chosen items (`AGC 031 E`), or
   - Creates $O(N^2)$ dense edges with absolute-value cost $K(i, j) = -(|x_i - x_j| + |y_i - y_j|)$ (`AGC 034 D`).

### 1.2 The Two-Part Unification Principle of Chapter 20

Every model in this chapter is governed by a single two-stage algebraic compilation framework:

::: {.callout-important title="The Chapter 20 Unification Spine: Supply–Demand Splitting & Kernel Factorization"}
1. **Part I — Bipartite Supply–Demand Decoupling (`拆点供需`)**:
   Whenever entity $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ has a mandatory throughput $r_i$ (e.g., $r_i = 1$ for cycle/path covers, $r_i = \text{daily demand}$ for inventory refurbishment) that transforms an incoming "ready" state into an outgoing "used/departing" state, we split $i$ into two **unlinked** ports in a bipartite supply–demand graph:
   - **Outgoing Supply Port $i_{\text{out}} \in \mathcal{S}$**: Fed directly from the source via $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } r_i, \text{cost } 0} i_{\text{out}}$, representing the $r_i$ units of outgoing state generated by $i$.
   - **Incoming Demand Port $i_{\text{in}} \in \mathcal{D}$**: Draining directly into the sink via $i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } r_i, \text{cost } 0} T$, representing the $r_i$ units of incoming state required by $i$.
   Crucially, there is **no forward edge $i_{\text{out}} \to i_{\text{in}}$** (unless a self-loop is a legal paid transition). Because the sink cut has capacity $\sum_{i=1}^N r_i$, any flow of volume $\sum_{i=1}^N r_i$ from $S$ to $T$ must saturate every demand port $j_{\text{in}} \to T$ using flow routed across valid cross-transitions $i_{\text{out}} \to j_{\text{in}}$ (or external start/purchase arcs $S \to j_{\text{in}}$).

2. **Part II — Transition Kernel Factorization Through Intermediate Hubs ($\mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{D}$)**:
   Whenever the effective transition cost $K(i, j)$ between supply $i \in \mathcal{S}$ and demand/target $j \in \mathcal{D}$ can be expressed as an infimum (or supremum for max-cost flow) over an intermediate index set $\mathcal{H}$:
   $$\boxed{K(i, j) = \min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \Big(\alpha(i, h) + \beta(h, j)\Big),}$$
   we replace the direct $\mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{D}$ transition layer by a layer of **intermediate hubs $h \in \mathcal{H}$** with directed arcs $i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\alpha(i, h)} h \xrightarrow{\beta(h, j)} j_{\text{in}}$. In any min-cost flow, a unit of flow routed from $i_{\text{out}}$ to $j_{\text{in}}$ automatically chooses the optimal hub $h^* \in \mathcal{H}$ achieving $\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} (\alpha(i, h) + \beta(h, j)) = K(i, j)$!
:::

### 1.3 Master Classification of Chapter 20 Models Under the Spine

The table below shows how all four sections and all eight ladder problems (`#153`–`#160`) instantiate this exact spine:

| Section & Flagship Archetype | Supply Port $\mathcal{S}$ ($S \to i_{\text{out}}$) | Demand Port $\mathcal{D}$ ($j_{\text{in}} \to T$) | Intermediate Hub / Factorization Kernel $\mathcal{H}$ | Graph Sparsification / Structural Payoff |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **§2: Cycle & Path Covers** (`#153`, `#157`) | Departure port $u_{\text{out}}$ (`cap 1`) | Arrival port $v_{\text{in}}$ (`cap 1`) | Direct transitions $u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{w_{uv}} v_{\text{in}}$ $\oplus$ Fleet Starter Hub $S \xrightarrow{K} H_{\text{start}} \xrightarrow{A_v} v_{\text{in}}$ | Exact cycle cover on general digraphs; exact $\le K$-path cover on DAGs (`#157`). |
| **§3: Delayed Resource Reuse & Caching** (`#155`, `#158`) | Evening Dirty Supply $d_t$ (`cap` $r_t$) | Morning Clean Demand $c_t$ (`cap` $r_t$) | Dirty holdover chain $d_t \xrightarrow{0} d_{t+1}$ + Laundry jumps $d_t \xrightarrow{f} c_{t+m}$, $d_t \xrightarrow{s} c_{t+n}$ + Fresh $S \xrightarrow{p} c_t$ | Decouples consumption from generation (`FM-20a`); only $O(N)$ arcs instead of $O(N^2)$ pairs! |
| **§4: Reverse Queue Slots & Lazy Spawning** (`#154`, `#156`) | Dish / Car Supply $i$ (`cap` $p_i$) |Sink $T$ (`cap` $\sum p_i$) | **Reverse Queue-Position Hubs** $h = (j, r)$: $\alpha\big(i, (j, r)\big) = r \cdot T_{i,j}$, $\beta\big((j, r), T\big) = 0$ (`cap 1`) | Multipliers $r \in \{1..k_j\}$ become static constants (`FM-20b`); lazy spawning keeps $\le P + M$ hubs active! |
| **§5.1: 2D Order-Statistic Rank Hubs** (`#159` `AGC 031 E`) | $X$-Rank Slot $X_r$ (`cap 1`, $r \in \{1..k\}$) | $Y$-Rank Slot $Y_q$ (`cap 1`, $q \in \{1..k\}$) | **Split Jewel Hubs** $i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{1, -v_i} i_{\text{out}}$ gated by $[L_r, R_r]$ and $[D_q, U_q]$ | Glues two laminar/transversal matroids $\mathcal{M}_X \cap \mathcal{M}_Y$ in series; uncrossed by Theorem 5.1. |
| **§5.2: 4-Sign Manhattan Hubs** (`#160` `AGC 034 D`) | Red Pile $R_i$ (`cap` $c_i$) | Blue Pile $B_j$ (`cap` $d_j$) | **4 Sign Hubs $H_{s_1, s_2}$** ($s_1, s_2 \in \{\pm 1\}$): $\alpha = -(s_1 x_i + s_2 y_i)$, $\beta = s_1 x'_j + s_2 y'_j$ | Compresses $N^2 = 10^6$ bipartite edges into $8N = 8,000$ hub edges! |

## 2. Min-Cost Cycle Covers & Degree-Constrained Path Covers (`循环格`, `星际竞速` & `营救皮卡丘`)

### 2.1 Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

How do you recognize that a routing, grid arrow-flipping, or multi-vehicle scheduling problem is a Bipartite Cycle Cover or Bounded-Fleet Path Cover?

- **Surface Clues**:
  1. *"Modify/select edges in a directed graph (or grid where every cell points to a neighbor) at minimum cost so that every vertex has in-degree $1$ and out-degree $1$ (so every cell lies on a cycle)."* (**[TJOI2013] Cyclic Grid `循环格`, `#153`**)
  2. *"Visit every vertex of a DAG (or precedence-ordered metric space) exactly once using at most $K$ agents (or arbitrary teleports of cost $A_v$), minimizing total travel + teleport cost."* (**[SDOI2010] Star Racing `星际竞速`**, **[ZJOI2011] Rescuing Pikachu `营救皮卡丘`, `#157`**)
- **Why TSP / Subset DP Fails**:
  The Travelling Salesperson Problem (requiring a *single* cycle of length $N$ on a general graph) is NP-hard and requires $O(2^N N^2)$ Held–Karp DP, which fails for $N \ge 25$. However, whenever:
  - **Regime A (Cycle Cover)**: The problem allows *any* partition of the $N$ vertices into vertex-disjoint directed cycles ($C_1 \sqcup C_2 \sqcup \dots \sqcup C_m = V$), OR
  - **Regime B (DAG Path Cover)**: The underlying transition graph is a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)** (where directed cycles are topologically impossible, so any degree-$\le 1$ subgraph automatically decomposes into open directed paths!),
  the global connectivity constraint disappears, and the problem reduces to a polynomial-time $O(N)$ Bipartite Matching / Min-Cost Flow problem!

### 2.2 Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation & The Component-Merging Invariant

Let $G = (V, E)$ be a directed graph on $N = |V|$ vertices with edge costs $c(u, v)$, and let $x_{u,v} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicate whether directed arc $(u, v) \in E$ is selected.

#### Case 1: Exact Vertex-Disjoint Directed Cycle Cover

A subset of directed edges $F = \{(u, v) \in E : x_{u,v} = 1\}$ is a vertex-disjoint union of directed cycles covering all of $V$ if and only if every vertex $u \in V$ has out-degree $1$ and every vertex $v \in V$ has in-degree $1$:

$$\sum_{v : (u, v) \in E} x_{u,v} = 1 \quad (\forall u \in V), \qquad \sum_{u : (u, v) \in E} x_{u,v} = 1 \quad (\forall v \in V), \qquad x_{u,v} \in \{0, 1\}.$$

Notice the algebraic structure: every variable $x_{u,v}$ appears with coefficient $+1$ in exactly one row of the first group (indexed by $u \in V_{\text{out}}$) and $+1$ in exactly one row of the second group (indexed by $v \in V_{\text{in}}$). This is the exact node-arc incidence system of a **Minimum-Cost Bipartite Perfect Matching** between $V_{\text{out}}$ and $V_{\text{in}}$!

#### Case 2: DAG Path Cover & The Component-Merging Invariant

Now suppose $G = (V, E)$ is a **DAG**, and we want to cover all $N$ vertices with vertex-disjoint directed paths. In any collection of vertex-disjoint paths covering $V$:

- Every vertex $u \in V$ is exited by at most one path edge: $\sum_{v : (u, v) \in E} x_{u,v} \le 1$.
- Every vertex $v \in V$ is entered by at most one path edge: $\sum_{u : (u, v) \in E} x_{u,v} \le 1$.
- Introduce binary slack indicator $s_v \in \{0, 1\}$ for each $v \in V$, where $s_v = 1$ if and only if vertex $v$ has in-degree $0$—that is, **$v$ is the starting vertex (head) of a new path**! Then every vertex $v \in V$ satisfies the exact arrival conservation equation:

$$\boxed{s_v + \sum_{u : (u, v) \in E} x_{u,v} = 1 \qquad (\forall v \in V).}$$

Summing this equation over all $v \in V$ yields the fundamental **Component-Merging Invariant**:

$$\underbrace{\sum_{v \in V} s_v}_{\text{Total Number of Paths } P} + \underbrace{\sum_{(u,v) \in E} x_{u,v}}_{\text{Total Internal Edges Used } M_{\text{used}}} = N \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad P = N - \sum_{(u,v) \in E} x_{u,v}.$$

In words: we start with $N$ isolated $1$-vertex paths; each chosen DAG edge $x_{u,v} = 1$ merges the path ending at $u$ with the path starting at $v$, reducing the total number of paths $P = \sum_{v \in V} s_v$ by exactly $1$.

- **Unbounded Fleet with Teleportation Start Costs (`[SDOI2010] 星际竞速`)**: Starting a path at $v$ ($s_v = 1$) costs $A_v$, and traversing edge $(u, v)$ ($x_{u,v} = 1$) costs $w_{u,v}$. We minimize $\sum_{v \in V} A_v s_v + \sum_{(u,v) \in E} w_{u,v} x_{u,v}$ subject to $s_v + \sum_u x_{u,v} = 1$ and $\sum_v x_{u,v} \le 1$.
- **Bounded Fleet of $\le K$ Vehicles (`ICPC WF 2015 Catering` / `[ZJOI2011] 营救皮卡丘`)**: If at most $K$ vehicles are available at a central depot $0$, then the total number of path starts is bounded by:

$$\sum_{v \in V} s_v \le K \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \sum_{(u,v) \in E} x_{u,v} \ge N - K.$$

### 2.3 Step 3 — Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)

Split each vertex $v \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ into an outgoing supply port $v_{\text{out}} \in \mathcal{S}$ and an incoming demand port $v_{\text{in}} \in \mathcal{D}$:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S(["Source S"]) -->|"cap K, cost 0"| H["Starter Hub H_start"]
    H -->|"cap 1, cost start_v"| Vin["v_in (Demand Port)"]
    S -->|"cap 1, cost 0"| Uout["u_out (Supply Port)"]
    Uout -->|"cap 1, cost c(u,v)"| Vin
    Vin -->|"cap 1, cost 0"| T(["Sink T"])
```

| Model Variant | Supply Side ($\mathcal{S}$) | Transition / Hub Layer ($\mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{D}$) | Demand Side ($\mathcal{D}$) & Target Flow |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Exact Directed Cycle Cover** (`#153`) | $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} u_{\text{out}}$ ($\forall u \in V$) | $u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } c(u,v)} v_{\text{in}}$ for $(u, v) \in E$ | $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} T$; require exact flow $F = N$. |
| **2. Unbounded-Fleet DAG Path Cover with Teleport Cost $A_v$** (`星际竞速`) | $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} u_{\text{out}}$ ($\forall u \in V$) | • DAG edges: $u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } w_{uv}} v_{\text{in}}$<br>• Teleport starts ($s_v = 1$): $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } A_v} v_{\text{in}}$ | $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} T$; require exact flow $F = N$. |
| **3. Bounded-Fleet ($\le K$) DAG Path Cover** (`#157` `营救皮卡丘`) | • $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} u_{\text{out}}$ ($\forall u \in V$)<br>• **Starter Hub**: $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } K, \text{cost } 0} H_{\text{start}}$ | • Relocations: $u_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } D(u,v)} v_{\text{in}}$ ($u < v$)<br>• Depot starts ($s_v = 1$): $H_{\text{start}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } D(0,v)} v_{\text{in}}$ | $v_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} T$; require exact flow $F = N$. |

::: {.callout-tip title="Precedence-Locked Metric Closure via Restricted Floyd–Warshall (`[ZJOI2011] 营救皮卡丘`, `#157`)"}
In **Luogu P4542 (`#157`)**, $K$ agents start at depot $0$ in an undirected weighted graph on $\{0, 1, \dots, N\}$ and must visit vertices $1, \dots, N$ such that **vertex $v$ cannot be unlocked until all vertices $1, 2, \dots, v-1$ have been visited**, and an agent travelling from an already-unlocked vertex $u < v$ to unlock $v$ **cannot pass through any still-locked vertex $w > v$**.

- Why does standard all-pairs Floyd–Warshall fail? Because the unconstrained shortest path $d(u, v)$ might detour through a high-numbered vertex $w > v$ that is still locked when the agent moves from $u$ to $v$!
- **Exact Fix**: During the outer loop $k = 0, 1, \dots, N$ of Floyd–Warshall, record the **precedence-restricted distance** $D(u, v)$ for $0 \le u < v \le N$ by allowing intermediate transitions through $k$ **only when $k \le \max(u, v) = v$**:
  $$D(u, v) = \text{shortest path from } u \text{ to } v \text{ using only internal vertices in } \{0, 1, \dots, v\}.$$
  Once $D(u, v)$ is precomputed in $O(N^3)$ time, the undirected graph becomes a transitive DAG on $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with edge weights $D(u, v)$ ($u < v$) and depot start weights $D(0, v)$, compiling directly into Row 3 of the table above!
:::

### 2.4 Step 4 — Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Subtour / Odd-Cycle Failure Modes

#### Concrete Toy Trace: DAG Path Cover (`N = 3`, Fleet Limit `K = 2`)

Suppose we have $N = 3$ targets $\{1, 2, 3\}$ and $K = 2$ agents at depot $0$.
- Depot start costs: $D(0, 1) = 5$, $D(0, 2) = 8$, $D(0, 3) = 9$.
- DAG transition costs ($u < v$): $D(1, 2) = 2$, $D(2, 3) = 6$, $D(1, 3) = 3$.
- We need $F = 3$ units of flow into $T$ via $1_{\text{in}}, 2_{\text{in}}, 3_{\text{in}}$.
  - If we used $1$ agent ($0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3$), the cost would be $D(0, 1) + D(1, 2) + D(2, 3) = 5 + 2 + 6 = 13$.
  - With $K = 2$ agents available at $H_{\text{start}}$, the MCMF network routes:
    1. $S \to H_{\text{start}} \xrightarrow{5} 1_{\text{in}} \to T$ (Agent 1 starts at $1$, cost $5$),
    2. $S \to 1_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{3} 3_{\text{in}} \to T$ (Agent 1 continues $1 \to 3$, cost $3$),
    3. $S \to H_{\text{start}} \xrightarrow{8} 2_{\text{in}} \to T$ (Agent 2 starts at $2$, cost $8$).
  -Wait: $5 + 3 + 8 = 16 > 13$, so the solver actually prefers using **only $1$ unit** from $H_{\text{start}}$ ($0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3$, cost $13$)! What if $D(0, 2) = 3$ instead of $8$? Then Agent 1 takes $0 \xrightarrow{5} 1 \xrightarrow{3} 3$ (cost $8$) and Agent 2 takes $0 \xrightarrow{3} 2$ (cost $3$), achieving total cost $11 < 13$. Because $S \to H_{\text{start}}$ has capacity $K = 2$ and cost $0$, the network automatically chooses the optimal number of active agents $P \in \{1, \dots, K\}$!

#### Broken Gadget Counterexamples (When Does $V_{\text{out}} \to V_{\text{in}}$ Fail?)

1. **The Cyclic Subtour Trap (Applying Bounded-Fleet Path Cover to a Non-DAG)**:
   Suppose $G$ is a **cyclic** graph consisting of a zero-cost triangle $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1$ ($c = 0$) that is unreachable from depot $0$ except via $D(0, v) = 100$ for $v \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, and we ask for $K = 1$ agent starting at $0$ to visit $\{1, 2, 3\}$.
   - In the bipartite network $V_{\text{out}} \to V_{\text{in}}$, the solver pushes $3$ units of flow around the detached cycle $1_{\text{out}} \to 2_{\text{in}}, 2_{\text{out}} \to 3_{\text{in}}, 3_{\text{out}} \to 1_{\text{in}}$ at **cost $0$**, using $0$ units from $H_{\text{start}}$!
   - **Why it broke**: A closed cycle of length $L$ supplies its own $L$ units of in-degree from its own $L$ units of out-degree ($s_v = 0$ for all $v$ on the cycle). Thus, the Component-Merging Invariant $P = N - \sum x_{u,v}$ is valid **if and only if the chosen transitions $x_{u,v} = 1$ cannot form a detached cycle**—which holds when $G$ is a DAG, or when the objective explicitly asks for a cycle cover (`#153`)!
2. **The Undirected Odd-Cycle Half-Integrality Trap**:
   Suppose $G = (V, E)$ is a **non-bipartite undirected** graph and we want a minimum-weight $1$-factor (undirected perfect matching) or $2$-factor (undirected cycle cover). If we replace each undirected edge $\{u, v\}$ by directed arcs $u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}$ and $v_{\text{out}} \to u_{\text{in}}$ in the bipartite split graph, a single undirected edge $\{u, v\}$ can be used in **both directions** ($1 \leftrightarrow 2$, a degenerate 2-cycle), or an odd triangle $(1, 2, 3)$ can form a directed 3-cycle $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1$ corresponding to a half-integral $1$-factor $x_e = 1/2$! Undirected matching / $2$-factors on non-bipartite graphs require Edmonds's Blossom algorithm (`Ch 22`), whereas **directed** cycle covers (`#153`) are $100\%$ exact via bipartite MCMF.

## 3. Time-Delayed Resource Reuse & Inventory Splitting (`[网络流24题] 餐巾计划` `#155` & `CF 802 C` `#158`)

### 3.1 Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Let us examine the landmark Chinese OI model **[Luogu P1251 / 网络流 24 题 #09] Napkin Plan (`餐巾计划问题`, `#155`)**:

- **Problem Mechanics**: A restaurant operates over $N \le 2,000$ days. Day $t \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ requires $r_t$ clean napkins. At the end of day $t$, the $r_t$ used napkins become **dirty** and can be:
  1. Held over as dirty napkins to the end of day $t + 1$ (cost $0$),
  2. Sent to the **fast laundry**, taking $m$ days at cost $f$ per napkin (ready as clean napkins on the morning of day $t + m$),
  3. Sent to the **slow laundry**, taking $n$ days at cost $s$ per napkin (ready as clean napkins on the morning of day $t + n$), or
  4. Left unwashed at the end of day $N$.
  In addition, on any morning $t$, the restaurant can buy **new clean napkins** at cost $p$ per napkin. Minimize total cost over the $N$ days.
- **Why Greedy Fails**:
  Whether a dirty napkin from day $t$ should be fast-washed (for day $t+m$), slow-washed (for day $t+n$), or held over to day $t+1$ (to be slow-washed for day $t+1+n$) depends on the global demand spikes across the entire future timeline $[t+m, N]$.
- **Why DP Fails**:
  The state at day $t$ would have to record the vector of dirty napkins currently in transit for the next $\max(m, n)$ days, which has $O((\sum r_t)^{\max(m, n)})$ states.

### 3.2 Broken-Gadget Counterexample `FM-20a`: Why a Single Vertex per Day Short-Circuits

Why can't we build a simple $N$-vertex timeline $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_N$ (one vertex per day $t$), inject fresh purchases $S \xrightarrow{\infty, p} v_t$, add laundry edges $v_t \xrightarrow{\infty, f} v_{t+m}$ and $v_t \xrightarrow{\infty, s} v_{t+n}$, and require $v_t \xrightarrow{r_t, 0} T$?

::: {.callout-warning title="Broken-Gadget Counterexample `FM-20a` ($\leftrightarrow$ `H-20B`) — The Single-Vertex Per Day Short-Circuit Trap"}
Suppose we use a single vertex $v_t$ for Day $t$. Look at what happens to a unit of flow at $v_t$:

1. **Attempt 1 (Demand Drain $v_t \xrightarrow{r_t, 0} T$ Without Re-Injection)**:
   If satisfying day $t$'s demand sends $r_t$ units of flow out of $v_t$ into the sink $T$, then by flow conservation at $v_t$, those $r_t$ napkins have **permanently exited the network at $T$**! Zero flow remains at $v_t$ to traverse the laundry arcs $v_t \to v_{t+m}$ or $v_t \to v_{t+n}$. Every napkin can be used only once!
2. **Attempt 2 (Injecting Both $S \xrightarrow{r_t, 0} v_t$ and $v_t \xrightarrow{r_t, 0} T$ at the Same Vertex $v_t$)**:
   Suppose a student tries to fix Attempt 1 by also injecting day $t$'s $r_t$ newly generated dirty napkins at the *same* vertex $v_t$ via $S \xrightarrow{r_t, 0} v_t$.
   - Immediately, the $r_t$ units of dirty supply from $S \xrightarrow{r_t, 0} v_t$ flow straight out through $v_t \xrightarrow{r_t, 0} T$ on the **same day $t$ at total cost $0$**!
   - Physically, dirty napkins generated at the *end* of day $t$ have travelled backward in time to satisfy the clean demand at the *start* of day $t$ without being washed!

**Root Cause**: At a single vertex $v_t$, flow conservation $\text{In}(v_t) = \text{Out}(v_t)$ cannot distinguish between a **clean napkin arriving in the morning** and a **dirty napkin departing in the evening**.
:::

### 3.3 Step 2 & Step 3 — Algebraic Derivation of the Dirty/Clean Split $(d_t \in \mathcal{S}, c_t \in \mathcal{D})$

We can derive the exact bipartite split graph from first principles in two complementary ways:

#### Derivation A: Direct Bipartite Conservation Pools (Dirty Supply $d_t \in \mathcal{S}$ vs. Clean Demand $c_t \in \mathcal{D}$)

Decouple day $t \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ into two independent conservation pools:

1. **Evening Dirty Supply Pool $d_t \in \mathcal{S}$**:
   At the end of day $t$, the restaurant generates $r_t$ dirty napkins. Let:
   - $w_t^{\text{hold}} \ge 0$ be the dirty napkins carried over from night $t$ to night $t+1$ (cost $0$),
   - $w_t^{\text{fast}} \ge 0$ be the dirty napkins sent from night $t$ to clean morning $t+m$ (cost $f$),
   - $w_t^{\text{slow}} \ge 0$ be the dirty napkins sent from night $t$ to clean morning $t+n$ (cost $s$).
   Since at most $r_t$ new dirty napkins are created on night $t$ (any unwashed napkins at the end of the horizon are simply left unused), the dirty pool conservation inequality at night $t$ is:
   $$w_t^{\text{hold}} + w_t^{\text{fast}} + w_t^{\text{slow}} - w_{t-1}^{\text{hold}} \le r_t \qquad (\forall t = 1, \dots, N).$$
   In flow language: source $S$ supplies **at most $r_t$ units** into dirty vertex $d_t$ via $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } r_t, \text{cost } 0} d_t$!

2. **Morning Clean Demand Pool $c_t \in \mathcal{D}$**:
   On the morning of day $t$, the restaurant must assemble **exactly $r_t$** clean napkins from fresh purchases $b_t \ge 0$ (cost $p$), fast laundry arriving from night $t - m$, and slow laundry arriving from night $t - n$:
   $$b_t + w_{t-m}^{\text{fast}} + w_{t-n}^{\text{slow}} = r_t \qquad (\forall t = 1, \dots, N).$$
   In flow language: clean vertex $c_t$ drains **exactly $r_t$ units** into the sink $T$ via $c_t \xrightarrow{\text{cap } r_t, \text{cost } 0} T$!

#### Derivation B: Lower-Bound Demand Substitution on the Continuous Napkin Timeline

What if we originally thought of a napkin as a continuous token flowing through a mandatory usage bridge $c_t \xrightarrow{[r_t, r_t]} d_t$ (lower bound $L = r_t$, upper bound $U = r_t$, cost $0$) on day $t$, with a disposal arc $d_N \xrightarrow{\infty, 0} T_{\text{real}}$ at the end of day $N$?

By Chapter 04's **Lower-Bound Demand Substitution** ($f(c_t \to d_t) = r_t$), fixing the flow on edge $c_t \to d_t$ to $r_t$ removes the edge $c_t \to d_t$ and replaces it with:
- A mandatory **excess supply of $+r_t$ at $d_t$**, which compiles to the super-source arc $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } r_t, \text{cost } 0} d_t$, and
- A mandatory **deficit demand of $-r_t$ at $c_t$**, which compiles to the super-sink arc $c_t \xrightarrow{\text{cap } r_t, \text{cost } 0} T$!

Thus the Lower-Bound Circulation Model and the Bipartite Dirty/Clean Split Model are **algebraically identical**!

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S(["Source S"]) -->|"cap r_t, cost 0"| Dt["Dirty Supply d_t"]
    S -->|"cap inf, cost p"| Ct["Clean Demand c_t"]
    Dt -->|"cap inf, cost 0"| Dt1["Dirty Supply d_{t+1}"]
    Dt -->|"cap inf, cost f"| Ctm["Clean Demand c_{t+m}"]
    Dt -->|"cap inf, cost s"| Ctn["Clean Demand c_{t+n}"]
    Ct -->|"cap r_t, cost 0"| T(["Sink T"])
```

| Arc Type | Directed Edge | Capacity | Unit Cost | Physical & Algebraic Meaning |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Dirty Generation** | $S \to d_t$ | $r_t$ | $0$ | Day $t$ generates up to $r_t$ dirty napkins after usage. |
| **Clean Consumption** | $c_t \to T$ | $r_t$ | $0$ | Day $t$ consumes $r_t$ clean napkins (saturated when $F = \sum r_t$). |
| **Fresh Purchase** | $S \to c_t$ | $\infty$ | $p$ | Buy $b_t$ brand-new clean napkins on morning $t$. |
| **Dirty Holdover** | $d_t \to d_{t+1}$ | $\infty$ | $0$ | Store dirty napkins from night $t$ to night $t+1$ ($t < N$). |
| **Fast Laundry** | $d_t \to c_{t+m}$ | $\infty$ | $f$ | Wash dirty napkins from night $t$ in $m$ days ($t + m \le N$). |
| **Slow Laundry** | $d_t \to c_{t+n}$ | $\infty$ | $s$ | Wash dirty napkins from night $t$ in $n$ days ($t + n \le N$). |

::: {.callout-caution title="Subtle Failure Guard: Why You Must NEVER Add a Disposal Edge $d_t \to T$ in the Split Graph"}
A frequent mistake when coding `Luogu P1251` is thinking: *"Dirty napkins left over on night $N$ are thrown away, so I should add a disposal edge $d_N \to T$ with `(cap = \infty, cost = 0)`."*

**Why this fails**: In the split network, $T$ is the super-sink that measures **how many clean demands $c_t \to T$ have been satisfied**. If you add $d_N \xrightarrow{\infty, 0} T$, the solver routes all $\sum_{t=1}^N r_t$ units of flow along the zero-cost path $S \xrightarrow{0} d_t \xrightarrow{0} \cdots \xrightarrow{0} d_N \xrightarrow{0} T$, reporting a max flow of $\sum r_t$ at **total cost $0$** while buying $0$ clean napkins!

In the split network, throwing away a dirty napkin on night $t$ is represented automatically by **leaving the supply arc $S \to d_t$ unsaturated**: because every flow path reaching $T$ must end at some $c_{t'} \to T$ (total capacity $\sum r_t$), only dirty napkins that are *actually laundered* into some $c_{t'}$ are ever pulled through $S \to d_t$!
:::

### 3.4 Step 4 — Hand-Checkable Toy Trace (`N = 3` Days) & Extension to $K$-Slot Caching (`#158`)

#### Numerical Toy Trace (`N = 3`, Demands `r = [3, 2, 4]`)

Suppose $N = 3$ days with demands $r = [3, 2, 4]$ (total required flow $F = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9$), fresh purchase cost $p = 10$, fast laundry $(m = 1 \text{ day}, f = 6)$, and slow laundry $(n = 2 \text{ days}, s = 3)$.

1. **Day 1 ($c_1 \to T$, cap $3$)**: No laundry can arrive on Day 1 ($1 - m = 0$). All $3$ units must take $S \xrightarrow{10} c_1 \to T$ (cost $3 \times 10 = 30$).
2. **Day 2 ($c_2 \to T$, cap $2$)**: Can buy fresh ($S \xrightarrow{10} c_2$) or fast-wash from Day 1 ($S \to d_1 \xrightarrow{6} c_2$). Wait: should we fast-wash Day 1's $3$ dirty napkins for Day 2, or save them to **slow-wash** for Day 3?
   - Let's trace SSP:
     - First, $S \to d_1 \xrightarrow{3} c_3 \to T$ has unit cost $3$ (slow laundry from Day 1 to Day 3!). SSP pushes $\min(r_1, r_3) = \min(3, 4) = 3$ units along $S \to d_1 \xrightarrow{3} c_3 \to T$ (cost $3 \times 3 = 9$). Now $S \to d_1$ (cap $3$) is completely saturated!
     - Next, for the remaining $1$ unit of $c_3 \to T$, SSP uses fast laundry from Day 2: $S \to d_2 \xrightarrow{6} c_3 \to T$ (pushes $1$ unit, cost $6$).
     - Finally, for Day 2 ($c_2 \to T$, cap $2$), since $S \to d_1$ is already used for slow laundry to $c_3$ (and rerouting $d_1$ to $c_2$ via the residual path $S \to c_3 \xleftarrow{-3} d_1 \xrightarrow{+6} c_2$ would cost $10 - 3 + 6 = 13 > 10$, wait: buying fresh at $c_2$ costs $10$, whereas fast-washing $d_1 \to c_2$ and buying fresh at $c_3$ would cost $6 + 10 = 16 > 3 + 10 = 13$!), SSP buys $2$ fresh napkins on Day 2 via $S \xrightarrow{10} c_2 \to T$ (cost $2 \times 10 = 20$).
   - **Total Optimal Cost**: $30 + 9 + 6 + 20 = 65$ ($5$ fresh napkins bought on Days 1–2, $3$ slow-washed $d_1 \to c_3$, $1$ fast-washed $d_2 \to c_3$, and $1$ dirty napkin from $d_2$ + $4$ from $d_3$ left unpulled at $S \to d_t$).

#### Extension: Weighted $K$-Slot Caching (**Codeforces 802 C — Heidi and Library (hard), `#158`**)

In **Codeforces 802 C (`#158`)**, a library cache holds at most $K$ books ($N, K \le 80$). On day $t \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, book $a_t$ is requested: if $a_t$ is already in the cache from an earlier day, cost is $0$; otherwise we must buy $a_t$ at cost $c_{a_t}$ (evicting a cached book if the cache is full).

Just like `餐巾计划`, we can compile this in two ways:
1. **Split-Request Token Routing (`20.2` Direct Split)**: Split request $t$ into $t_{\text{in}}$ and $t_{\text{out}}$ (enforcing that $a_t$ is present on day $t$). Keeping book $a_t$ in cache until its next occurrence $\text{next}(t)$ is a direct reuse chord $t_{\text{out}} \to \text{next}(t)_{\text{in}}$ of capacity $1$ that saves re-buying $a_t$ on day $\text{next}(t)$!
2. **Timeline Saving Chords (Compressed Equation-Difference Form)**: Even more compactly, pay the baseline cost $\text{Base} = \sum_{t=1}^N c_{a_t}$ upfront (assuming every request buys its book fresh). On any day $s$, the requested book $a_s$ occupies $1$ mandatory cache slot, leaving **$K - 1$ background cache slots** for books retained across day $s$. Retaining book $a_t$ from day $t$ to its next request $t' = \text{next}(t)$ occupies $1$ background slot on days $s \in \{t+1, \dots, t'-1\}$ and **saves $c_{a_t}$**:
   - Build a timeline spine $1 \to 2 \to \dots \to N$ where each edge $s \to s+1$ has `(cap = K - 1, cost = 0)`.
   - If $\text{next}(t) = t + 1$, book $a_t$ is requested again immediately tomorrow, saving $c_{a_t}$ unconditionally with $0$ background slots!
   - If $\text{next}(t) > t + 1$, add a saving chord $(t + 1) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -c_{a_t}} \text{next}(t)$.
   Both compilations are presented in full detail in Worked Problem `#158` (§6.6).


---

## 4. Reverse Queue-Position Factorization & Dynamic Lazy Node Spawning (`动态加点`: `[SCOI2007] 修车` `#154` & `[NOI2012] 美食节` `#156`)

### 4.1 Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

Consider a scheduling problem on heterogeneous parallel machines/chefs (**[SCOI2007] Car Repair `修车`, `#154`** and **[NOI2012] Food Festival `美食节`, `#156`**):

- **Problem Mechanics**: There are $N$ dish types (with order counts $p_1, \dots, p_N$, totaling $P = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i$ dishes; in `修车`, $p_i = 1$ so $P = N \le 60$; in `美食节`, $N \le 40$ and $P \le 800$) and $M$ chefs ($M \le 9$ in `修车`; $M \le 100$ in `美食节`). Chef $j \in \{1, \dots, M\}$ takes $T_{i,j} > 0$ time to cook one dish of type $i$. Each chef cooks their assigned dishes **sequentially one after another**. The waiting time of a dish is the time from $t = 0$ until that dish finishes cooking (i.e., the sum of cooking times of all dishes cooked by that chef before it, plus its own cooking time). Minimize the **total waiting time** (or average waiting time $\frac{1}{P} \sum C_d$) across all $P$ dishes.
- **Why Greedy Fails**: Assigning a dish to the chef who can finish it earliest right now ignores how that dish will delay all subsequent dishes assigned to the same chef later.
- **Why DP Fails**: Tracking the current completion time or queue length across $M \le 100$ chefs requires exponential state space.

### 4.2 Step 2 — The Waiting-Time Reverse-Indexing Identity & Broken-Gadget `FM-20b`

Suppose chef $j$ is assigned $k$ dishes in chronological order $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$ with cooking times $t_1, t_2, \dots, t_k$ (where $t_p = T_{d_p, j}$). Let us write out the waiting time of each dish in chef $j$'s queue:

- The $1\text{st}$ dish ($p = 1$) finishes at $t_1$.
- The $2\text{nd}$ dish ($p = 2$) waits for $d_1$ and finishes at $t_1 + t_2$.
- The $p\text{-th}$ dish finishes at $t_1 + t_2 + \dots + t_p$.

::: {.callout-warning title="Broken-Gadget Counterexample `FM-20b` — Why Forward Queue Indexing ($p = 1, 2, \dots, k$) Fails"}
Suppose a student creates queue slot vertices $(j, p)$ indexed in **forward chronological order** ($p = 1$ for the $1\text{st}$ dish cooked by chef $j$, $p = 2$ for the $2\text{nd}$ dish, $\dots$, $p = k$ for the $k\text{-th}$ dish).

How much does the $p\text{-th}$ dish $d_p$ contribute to the **total** waiting time $\sum_{q=1}^k (t_1 + \dots + t_q)$?
- Dish $d_1$ ($t_1$) appears in the completion time of $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$—so $t_1$ is multiplied by **$k$**!
- Dish $d_p$ ($t_p$) appears in the completion time of $d_p, d_{p+1}, \dots, d_k$—so $t_p$ is multiplied by **$(k - p + 1)$**!

Because the multiplier $(k - p + 1)$ of forward slot $p$ depends on the **unknown total number of dishes $k$** that chef $j$ will eventually cook, a forward-indexed edge $i \to (j, p)$ **cannot be assigned a fixed static cost** before solving the flow!
:::

How do we eliminate the unknown queue length $k$ from the multiplier? **Count positions backward from the end of chef $j$'s queue!**

Define the **reverse queue position** $r = k - p + 1 \in \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$:

- $r = 1$ is the **last** dish cooked by chef $j$ ($p = k$): it delays **only itself** ($1$ dish), so its cost contribution is $1 \cdot t_k$.
- $r = 2$ is the **second-to-last** dish cooked by chef $j$ ($p = k - 1$): it delays **itself and the last dish** ($2$ dishes), so its cost contribution is $2 \cdot t_{k-1}$.
- In general, the dish placed at **reverse position $r$ from the end** of chef $j$'s queue ($p = k - r + 1$) delays itself and the $r - 1$ dishes after it—contributing **exactly $r \cdot t_{k - r + 1}$** to the total waiting time, regardless of how many dishes precede it!

Algebraically, swapping the order of summation gives the foundational **Waiting-Time Reverse Factorization Identity**:

$$\boxed{\sum_{p=1}^k \big(t_1 + t_2 + \dots + t_p\big) = \sum_{p=1}^k (k - p + 1) \cdot t_p = \sum_{r=1}^k r \cdot t_{k - r + 1}.}$$

Under our Chapter 20 Unification Spine (§1.2), each reverse queue slot $h = (j, r) \in \{1, \dots, M\} \times \{1, \dots, P\}$ acts as a capacity-$1$ **intermediate hub**:

- **Supply Side ($\mathcal{S}$)**: Each dish type $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ receives $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } p_i, \text{cost } 0} i$.
- **Kernel Transition ($\mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{H}$)**: Assigning a dish of type $i$ to chef $j$'s $r$-th from last slot $(j, r)$ traverses the directed arc:
  $$i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } r \cdot T_{i,j}} (j, r).$$
- **Demand Side ($\mathcal{H} \to T$)**: Each reverse slot $(j, r)$ can hold at most $1$ dish across all types:
  $$(j, r) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } 0} T.$$

### 4.3 Step 3 — Frontier Slot Dominance & Dynamic Lazy Node Spawning (`动态加点`, `#156`)

In **[SCOI2007] Car Repair (`#154`)**, $P = N \le 60$ and $M \le 9$, so pre-allocating all $M \times N \le 540$ slot hubs $(j, r)$ creates $N^2 M \le 32,400$ edges—solving in $< 10\text{ ms}$.

Now look at **[NOI2012] Food Festival (`#156`)**, where $N \le 40$ dish types, $M \le 100$ chefs, and $P = \sum_{i=1}^N p_i \le 800$ total dishes (or variants where $N = P = 800, M = 40$):

- **The Static Graph Explosion**: Because a single chef could theoretically cook all $P = 800$ dishes, each of the $M = 100$ chefs has $P = 800$ potential reverse slots $(j, 1), \dots, (j, P)$. Pre-allocating all $M \cdot P = 80,000$ slot vertices and wiring every dish to every slot builds $N \cdot M \cdot P = 3.2 \times 10^6$ edges (or $P^2 M \approx 2.56 \times 10^7$ edges if dishes are individual nodes). Running $P = 800$ augmentations on millions of edges results in an immediate **Time Limit Exceeded (TLE)**!
- **The Key Sparsity Insight**: Across all $M = 100$ chefs combined, the total number of dishes cooked in the entire festival is **only $P = 800$**. At the end of the algorithm, out of the $80,000$ potential slot vertices $(j, r)$, **at most $P = 800$ slots are ever used; the remaining $79,200$ slots sit at flow $0$ forever!**

Why did we build $(j, 2), (j, 3), \dots, (j, 800)$ before $(j, 1)$ was even used? For each chef $j \in \{1, \dots, M\}$, define the **frontier rank $r_j \ge 1$** to be the smallest reverse rank on chef $j$ whose sink arc $(j, r_j) \to T$ is currently unsaturated.

::: {.callout-important title="Theorem 4.1 — Frontier Slot Dominance & The Dynamic Lazy Spawning Invariant (`动态加点`)"}
Suppose $T_{i,j} > 0$ for all $i, j$. At any stage of the Successive Shortest Path (SSP) algorithm, every shortest augmenting path from $S$ to $T$ uses **exclusively**:

1. **Already-saturated slots** $(j, s)$ with $1 \le s < r_j$ (which carry residual backward arcs $(j, s) \to i_{\text{old}}$ of cost $-s \cdot T_{i_{\text{old}}, j}$, allowing the solver to dynamically reorder or reassign previously scheduled dishes), and
2. **At most one frontier slot** $(j^*, r_{j^*})$ as its penultimate vertex immediately before $T$.

No shortest augmenting path can ever visit any higher unsaturated slot $(j, r)$ with $r > r_j$!

*Proof*:
1. For any unsaturated slot $(j, r)$ with $r \ge r_j$, the current flow on $(j, r) \to T$ is $0$. By flow conservation at $(j, r)$, the current flow on every incoming arc $i \to (j, r)$ is also $0$.
2. Therefore, in the residual network $G_f$, vertex $(j, r)$ has **zero outgoing residual arcs back to any dish node $i$**; its only outgoing residual arc is the sink edge $(j, r) \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} T$.
3. Consequently, any simple augmenting path from $S$ to $T$ that visits an unsaturated slot $(j, r)$ ($r \ge r_j$) must enter $(j, r)$ from some dish node $i$ and immediately exit to $T$:
   $$S \leadsto i \xrightarrow{r \cdot T_{i,j}} (j, r) \xrightarrow{0} T.$$
4. Because the frontier slot $(j, r_j)$ is also unsaturated, the path $S \leadsto i \xrightarrow{r_j \cdot T_{i,j}} (j, r_j) \xrightarrow{0} T$ is also residual-feasible and is **strictly cheaper** by $(r - r_j) \cdot T_{i,j} > 0$ for all $r > r_j$! $\blacksquare$
:::

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S(["Source S"]) -->|"cap p_i, cost 0"| Dish["Dish Type i"]
    Dish -->|"cap 1, cost 1*T_{i,j} (SATURATED)"| Slot1["Slot (j, 1)"]
    Slot1 -.->|"residual -1*T_{i',j} (reorders queue!)"| DishOld["Earlier Dish i'"]
    Slot1 -->|"flow 1/1"| T(["Sink T"])
    Dish -->|"cap 1, cost r_j*T_{i,j} (ACTIVE FRONTIER)"| SlotR["Frontier Slot (j, r_j)"]
    SlotR -->|"cap 1, cost 0 (saturating this spawns r_j+1!)"| T
```

#### The Dynamic Lazy Spawning Algorithm Contract (`[NOI2012] 美食节`, `#156`)

1. **Initialization ($0$ Flow)**:
   - Create $S$, $T$, the $N$ dish vertices $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ with $S \xrightarrow{p_i, 0} i$, and **only the $M$ rank-$1$ frontier slots $(j, 1)$** for $j \in \{1, \dots, M\}$.
   - Wire $i \xrightarrow{1,\; 1 \cdot T_{i,j}} (j, 1)$ for all $i, j$ and $(j, 1) \xrightarrow{1, 0} T$.
   - Initial active graph size: $N + M + 2 \le 142$ vertices and $N M + N + M \le 4,140$ directed edges!
2. **Single-Unit Augmentation + On-Demand Spawning ($f = 1, 2, \dots, P$)**:
   - Find the shortest augmenting path $P_f$ from $S$ to $T$ in the current active residual graph and push **$\Delta = 1$ unit of flow** along $P_f$.
   - Look at the penultimate vertex of $P_f$: because only frontier slots have unsaturated edges into $T$, the last edge of $P_f$ is guaranteed to be $(j^*, r_{j^*}) \to T$ for some unique chef $j^* \in \{1, \dots, M\}$.
   - **Immediate Lazy Spawn**: Increment $r_{j^*} \gets r_{j^*} + 1$, allocate a single new vertex $v_{\text{new}} = (j^*, r_{j^*})$, wire $v_{\text{new}} \xrightarrow{1, 0} T$, and wire $N$ incoming arcs:
     $$i \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1,\; \text{cost } r_{j^*} \cdot T_{i, j^*}} (j^*, r_{j^*}) \qquad (\forall i \in \{1, \dots, N\}).$$
   - *(If using Primal–Dual Dijkstra with Johnson potentials $\pi$, initialize the new vertex's potential in $O(N)$ time as $\pi(j^*, r_{j^*}) = \min_{1 \le i \le N}\big(\pi(i) + r_{j^*} \cdot T_{i, j^*}\big)$ so all reduced costs remain non-negative, or run SPFA on the tiny $\le 942$-vertex active graph!)*
3. **Final Graph Complexity**:
   After all $P \le 800$ dishes are scheduled, the total number of spawned slot vertices is **exactly $M + P \le 900$**, and the total number of directed edges ever created is:
   $$|E_{\text{active}}| = N(M + P) + N + M + P \le 40 \times 900 + 940 = 36,940 \text{ edges},$$
   shrinking the graph by **nearly $100\times$** and running in $< 0.05\text{ s}$!

::: {.callout-caution title="Implementation Trap: Why Zkw Multi-Push Blocking Flow Fails Without Inline Spawning"}
If you use a Dinic-style **multi-augmenting blocking flow** on the zero-reduced-cost DAG (Zkw MCMF) and wait until the *end* of the DFS phase to spawn $(j^*, r_{j^*} + 1)$, the algorithm can produce a **suboptimal cost**!

*Why?* Suppose Dish 1 has $p_1 = 2$, Chef 1 takes $T_{1,1} = 1$, and Chef 2 takes $T_{1,2} = 3$. If a phase pushes $2$ units of flow simultaneously before spawning $(1, 2)$ (which has cost $2 \cdot 1 = 2 < 3$), the second unit of Dish 1 cannot see $(1, 2)$ yet and is forced onto Chef 2 at cost $3$ instead of $(1, 2)$ at cost $2$!

**Rule**: Always push **$\Delta = 1$ unit of flow per shortest-path step** (or spawn $(j^*, r_{j^*} + 1)$ inline inside the DFS the exact instant $(j^*, r_{j^*}) \to T$ is saturated).
:::

### 4.4 Step 4 — Hand-Checkable Toy Trace: How Residual Backward Arcs Reorder a Chef's Queue!

A common question when first meeting reverse queue slots is: *"If Augmentation 1 puts Dish A into slot $(j, 1)$ (the LAST dish cooked by chef $j$), what if we later realize Dish A is super fast and should be cooked FIRST (at slot $(j, 2)$), while a slow Dish B should be cooked LAST (at slot $(j, 1)$)?"*

Let us trace a concrete 2-dish, 2-chef instance to watch the residual network **reorder Chef 2's queue automatically**:

- **Instance**: $P = 2$ cars (`Car 1`, `Car 2`), $M = 2$ mechanics (`Mech 1`, `Mech 2`).
  - `Car 1` repair times: $T_{1,1} = 10$ on `Mech 1`, $T_{1,2} = 2$ on `Mech 2`.
  - `Car 2` repair times: $T_{2,1} = 10$ on `Mech 1`, $T_{2,2} = 5$ on `Mech 2`.
- **Initial Active Slots**: $(1, 1)$ and $(2, 1)$.
- **Augmentation 1 ($f = 1$)**:
  - Shortest path from $S$ to $T$ is $S \to \text{Car } 1 \xrightarrow{1 \times 2 = 2} (2, 1) \to T$ of cost $+2$.
  - Now `Car 1` occupies $(2, 1)$ (last slot on `Mech 2`), creating the **residual backward arc** $(2, 1) \xrightarrow{-2} \text{Car } 1$.
  - Since $(2, 1) \to T$ is saturated, we **lazily spawn slot $(2, 2)$** with incoming arcs $\text{Car } 1 \xrightarrow{2 \times 2 = 4} (2, 2)$ and $\text{Car } 2 \xrightarrow{2 \times 5 = 10} (2, 2)$.
- **Augmentation 2 ($f = 2$, Scheduling `Car 2`)**:
  Look at the three residual paths available from $S \to \text{Car } 2$ to $T$:
  1. Put `Car 2` on `Mech 1` slot $(1, 1)$: $S \to \text{Car } 2 \xrightarrow{+10} (1, 1) \to T$ (cost $+10$).
  2. Put `Car 2` on `Mech 2` slot $(2, 2)$ (**before** `Car 1`, so slow `Car 2` delays fast `Car 1`!): $S \to \text{Car } 2 \xrightarrow{+10} (2, 2) \to T$ (cost $+10$).
  3. **Traverse the residual backward arc $(2, 1) \xrightarrow{-2} \text{Car } 1$ to swap `Car 1` into slot $(2, 2)$**:
     $$S \to \text{Car } 2 \xrightarrow{+5} (2, 1) \xrightarrow{-2} \text{Car } 1 \xrightarrow{+4} (2, 2) \to T \qquad (\text{net cost } = 5 - 2 + 4 = +7!).$$
- SSP selects Path 3 of cost $+7$, giving total waiting time $2 + 7 = 9$:
  - **Physical Result after Cancellation**: `Car 1` is moved to reverse slot $(2, 2)$ ($2\text{nd}$ from last = **cooked $1\text{st}$**, finishes at $t = 2$), and `Car 2` takes reverse slot $(2, 1)$ ($1\text{st}$ from last = **cooked $2\text{nd}$**, finishes at $t = 2 + 5 = 7$), for total waiting time $2 + 7 = 9$!
  - Notice why we must **never delete** already-saturated slot nodes $(j, s)$ ($s < r_j$): their residual backward arcs $(j, s) \to i_{\text{old}}$ are the exact mechanism that shifts fast jobs earlier in the queue when slower jobs arrive!

---

## 5. Non-Graph Geometric & Order-Statistic Hubs — 2D Rank Slots (`AGC 031 E` `#159`) & 4-Sign Manhattan Hubs (`AGC 034 D` `#160`)

We now apply the Chapter 20 **Transition Kernel Factorization Spine** ($\mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{D}$) to two landmark AtCoder Grand Contest problems that contain **zero graphs** in their problem statements.

### 5.1 Flagship I: 2D Order-Statistic Rank Hubs (`AtCoder AGC 031 E — Snuke the Phantom Thief`, `#159`)

#### Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

- **Problem Statement (`AGC 031 E`)**: There are $N \le 80$ jewels in the 2D plane at $(x_i, y_i)$ ($1 \le x_i, y_i \le 100$) with values $v_i \le 10^{15}$. Snuke wants to steal a subset of jewels of maximum total value subject to $M \le 320$ directional half-plane count constraints of 4 types:
  - Type `L` $(a_m, b_m)$: **At most $b_m$** stolen jewels have $x_i \le a_m$.
  - Type `R` $(a_m, b_m)$: **At most $b_m$** stolen jewels have $x_i \ge a_m$.
  - Type `D` $(a_m, b_m)$: **At most $b_m$** stolen jewels have $y_i \le a_m$.
  - Type `U` $(a_m, b_m)$: **At most $b_m$** stolen jewels have $y_i \ge a_m$.
- **Why 2D DP and Direct Submodular Cuts Fail**:
  - In general 2D subset selection, simultaneously enforcing upper bounds on prefix and suffix sums along both the $X$-axis and the $Y$-axis couples every jewel with two orthogonal families of half-planes.
  - Because `R` constraints bound the suffix $x \ge a_m$ while `L` constraints bound the prefix $x \le a_m$, we cannot even tell how many jewels are allowed in $(-\infty, a_m - 1]$ unless we know the **total number of stolen jewels $k$**!

#### Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Fixing $k$ Turns Count Bounds into Order-Statistic Intervals!

Look at the small constraint $N \le 80$: we can afford an outer loop over the **exact total number of stolen jewels $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$**!

Suppose Snuke steals **exactly $k$ jewels**. Sort the $k$ stolen jewels twice:
- Sort their $X$-coordinates in non-decreasing order: $x_{(1)} \le x_{(2)} \le \dots \le x_{(k)}$.
- Sort their $Y$-coordinates in non-decreasing order: $y_{(1)} \le y_{(2)} \le \dots \le y_{(k)}$.

Now watch what happens to each of the 4 constraint types when $k$ is fixed:

1. **Type `L` ("At most $b_m$ stolen jewels have $x \le a_m$")**:
   In the sorted sequence $x_{(1)} \le x_{(2)} \le \dots \le x_{(k)}$, saying that at most $b_m$ elements are $\le a_m$ is $100\%$ equivalent to saying that **the $(b_m + 1)$-th smallest element is strictly greater than $a_m$**:
   $$\text{Count}(x \le a_m) \le b_m \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \begin{cases} x_{(b_m + 1)} \ge a_m + 1 & \text{if } b_m + 1 \le k, \\ \text{vacuously true} & \text{if } b_m \ge k. \end{cases}$$

2. **Type `R` ("At most $b_m$ stolen jewels have $x \ge a_m$")**:
   Because the total number of stolen jewels is **fixed at $k$**, having at most $b_m$ jewels with $x \ge a_m$ is $100\%$ equivalent to having **at least $k - b_m$ jewels with $x \le a_m - 1$**—which means the $(k - b_m)$-th smallest element is at most $a_m - 1$:
   $$\text{Count}(x \ge a_m) \le b_m \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \begin{cases} x_{(k - b_m)} \le a_m - 1 & \text{if } k - b_m \ge 1, \\ \text{infeasible for this } k & \text{if } b_m < 0 \text{ (never)}. \end{cases}$$

3. **Types `D` and `U` on $y_{(1)} \le \dots \le y_{(k)}$**:
   By identical logic, Type `D` $(a_m, b_m)$ becomes $y_{(b_m + 1)} \ge a_m + 1$ (for $b_m + 1 \le k$), and Type `U` $(a_m, b_m)$ becomes $y_{(k - b_m)} \le a_m - 1$ (for $k - b_m \ge 1$).

#### The Interval Monotonization Recurrences

Furthermore, because $x_{(1)} \le x_{(2)} \le \dots \le x_{(k)}$ and $y_{(1)} \le y_{(2)} \le \dots \le y_{(k)}$, any lower bound on rank $r - 1$ is inherited by rank $r$, and any upper bound on rank $r + 1$ is inherited by rank $r$. We propagate all bounds across $r = 1, \dots, k$:

$$L_r = \max\!\Big(\{L_{r-1}\} \cup \{a_m + 1 : \text{type}_m = \texttt{'L'},\; b_m + 1 \le r\}\Big), \qquad R_r = \min\!\Big(\{R_{r+1}\} \cup \{a_m - 1 : \text{type}_m = \texttt{'R'},\; k - b_m \ge r\}\Big),$$

and analogously $[D_q, U_q]$ for each $Y$-rank $q \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. This produces $k$ **monotone $X$-intervals** $[L_r, R_r]$ and $k$ **monotone $Y$-intervals** $[D_q, U_q]$ satisfying:

$$\boxed{L_1 \le L_2 \le \dots \le L_k, \quad R_1 \le R_2 \le \dots \le R_k, \qquad D_1 \le D_2 \le \dots \le D_k, \quad U_1 \le U_2 \le \dots \le U_k.}$$

*(If $L_r > R_r$ or $D_r > U_r$ for any $r \in \{1, \dots, k\}$, then stealing $k$ jewels is immediately impossible!)*

#### Step 3 — 4-Layer MCMF Compilation & The Monotone Interval Uncrossing Theorem

For a fixed $k \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, we create:
- **Supply Side ($\mathcal{S}$)**: $k$ $X$-rank slot vertices $X_1, \dots, X_k$, each with $S \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} X_r$.
- **Intermediate Jewel Hubs ($\mathcal{H}$)**: Each jewel $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ is split into $i_{\text{in}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } -v_i} i_{\text{out}}$ (or shifted cost $V_{\max} - v_i \ge 0$).
- **Demand Side ($\mathcal{D}$)**: $k$ $Y$-rank slot vertices $Y_1, \dots, Y_k$, each with $Y_q \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} T$.
- **Interval Compatibility Edges**:
  - Wire $X_r \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} i_{\text{in}}$ if and only if $x_i \in [L_r, R_r]$.
  - Wire $i_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{\text{cap } 1, \text{cost } 0} Y_q$ if and only if $y_i \in [D_q, U_q]$.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S(["Source S"]) -->|"cap 1, cost 0"| Xr["X-Rank Slot X_r"]
    Xr -->|"cap 1, cost 0 (if L_r <= x_i <= R_r)"| Iin["Jewel i_in"]
    Iin -->|"cap 1, cost -v_i"| Iout["Jewel i_out"]
    Iout -->|"cap 1, cost 0 (if D_q <= y_i <= U_q)"| Yq["Y-Rank Slot Y_q"]
    Yq -->|"cap 1, cost 0"| T(["Sink T"])
```

Wait—when we match $k$ jewels to $X_1, \dots, X_k$ in this 4-layer network, nothing in the graph forces the jewel matched to $X_1$ to have a smaller $X$-coordinate than the jewel matched to $X_2$! Could the MCMF solver cheat by matching a jewel with $x = 10$ to $X_1$ and a jewel with $x = 5$ to $X_2$?

::: {.callout-important title="Theorem 5.1 — The Monotone Interval Uncrossing Theorem"}
Let $[L_1, R_1], \dots, [L_k, R_k]$ be monotone intervals ($L_1 \le \dots \le L_k$ and $R_1 \le \dots \le R_k$). For any $k$-element subset of jewels $J = \{i_1, \dots, i_k\}$ sorted as $x_{i_1} \le x_{i_2} \le \dots \le x_{i_k}$:

$$J \text{ has a perfect matching to } \{X_1, \dots, X_k\} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad x_{i_r} \in [L_r, R_r] \text{ for all } r \in \{1, \dots, k\}.$$

*Proof*:
$(\Leftarrow)$ is immediate: match $i_r$ to $X_r$.
$(\Rightarrow)$ Suppose $J$ has a valid matching $\pi : \{1, \dots, k\} \to J$ that contains an inversion: for some $p < q$, the matched jewels $u = \pi(p)$ and $w = \pi(q)$ satisfy $x_u > x_w$.
- Because $u$ is matched to $X_p$ and $w$ is matched to $X_q$, we have $L_p \le x_u \le R_p$ and $L_q \le x_w \le R_q$.
- Combining $x_w < x_u$ with the Monotone Interval Property $L_p \le L_q$ and $R_p \le R_q$ yields two chains of inequalities:
  $$L_p \le L_q \le x_w < x_u \le R_p \implies x_w \in [L_p, R_p],$$
  $$L_q \le x_w < x_u \le R_p \le R_q \implies x_u \in [L_q, R_q].$$
- Therefore, **both cross-edges $X_p \to w_{\text{in}}$ and $X_q \to u_{\text{in}}$ are also present in the graph**! Swapping the $X$-slot assignments of $u$ and $w$ preserves feasibility and keeps the chosen jewel set $J$ (and its total value $\sum_{i \in J} v_i$) $100\%$ unchanged. Repeating this uncrossing swap eliminates all inversions on both the $X$-side and the $Y$-side! $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Theoretical Boundary — Why 2D Rank Slots Work (`2-Matroid Intersection`) While 3D Rank Slots Are NP-Hard (`3-Matroid Intersection`)"}
Why does `AGC 031 E` compile to MCMF in 2D (`L, R, D, U`), and what would happen in 3D $(x_i, y_i, z_i)$ with 6 constraint types (`L, R, D, U, F, B`)?
- Along a single axis (say $X$), the family of $k$-subsets matchable to $[L_1, R_1], \dots, [L_k, R_k]$ forms the bases of a **Transversal / Laminar Matroid** $\mathcal{M}_X$.
- In **2D**, we are maximizing $\sum_{i \in J} v_i$ over the **2-Matroid Intersection** $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_X) \cap \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_Y)$, which glues $\mathcal{M}_X$ on the left of $i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}$ and $\mathcal{M}_Y$ on the right—forming a single series flow network!
- In **3D**, feasible subsets lie in the **3-Matroid Intersection** $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_X) \cap \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_Y) \cap \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{M}_Z)$. A single-commodity flow token passing through $i_{\text{in}} \to i_{\text{out}}$ has only **one entry port** ($X$) and **one exit port** ($Y$); it has no third port to simultaneously enforce a $1$-to-$1$ matching with $Z$-slots, and 3-Matroid Intersection is **strongly NP-hard**!
:::

#### Step 4 — Broken-Gadget Counterexamples for `AGC 031 E`

1. **Accepting Partial Flow $f < k$ During Trial $k$**:
   Because Type `R` and Type `U` constraints place upper bounds on rank $k - b_m$ (which explicitly depends on the assumed total cardinality $k$), the graph constructed for trial $k$ is **only valid if all $k$ rank slots are saturated ($\text{flow} = k$)**! If the max flow for trial $k$ is $f < k$, you must **discard** that trial completely (if $f$ jewels were actually valid, they would be found during the outer-loop iteration for $k' = f$).
2. **Omitting the Interval Monotonization Pass**:
   Suppose $k = 2$ and there is a single constraint `L` $(a = 10, b = 0)$, which says $x_{(1)} \ge 11$. If you only set $L_1 = 11$ without propagating $L_2 = \max(L_2, L_1) = 11$, then $[L_2, R_2]$ remains $[1, 100]$. The solver can then match a jewel at $x = 3$ to $X_2$ and a jewel at $x = 15$ to $X_1$, violating "at most $0$ jewels have $x \le 10$"!

---

### 5.2 Flagship II: 4-Sign Manhattan Hubs (`AtCoder AGC 034 D — Manhattan Max Matching`, `#160`)

#### Step 1 — Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)

- **Problem Statement (`AGC 034 D`)**: In the 2D plane, there are $N \le 1,000$ Red point piles at $(x_i, y_i)$ with $c_i$ red balls, and $N \le 1,000$ Blue point piles at $(x'_j, y'_j)$ with $d_j$ blue balls, where $\sum_{i=1}^N c_i = \sum_{j=1}^N d_j = S_{\text{tot}} \le 10^5$. Match all $S_{\text{tot}}$ red balls with blue balls to **maximize** the sum of Manhattan distances:
  $$\max \sum_{(i, j)} f_{i,j} \Big(|x_i - x'_j| + |y_i - y'_j|\Big).$$
- **Why Complete Bipartite MCMF TLEs**:
  Wiring every Red pile $R_i$ directly to every Blue pile $B_j$ creates $N^2 = 10^6$ edges. Running SSP across up to $S_{\text{tot}} \le 10^5$ units of flow on $10^6$ edges is far too slow.

#### Step 2 — Intermediate Algebraic Representation: Dual-Norm Sign Factorization

Why can we factor the non-linear Manhattan kernel $K_{\max}(i, j) = |x_i - x'_j| + |y_i - y'_j|$ when we are **maximizing** total distance?

For any real number $z \in \mathbb{R}$, $|z| = \max(z, -z) = \max_{s \in \{-1, +1\}} s \cdot z$. Therefore, in 2D ($d = 2$), the Manhattan distance between $(x_i, y_i)$ and $(x'_j, y'_j)$ is the pointwise maximum over all $2^2 = 4$ sign pairs $(s_1, s_2) \in \{-1, +1\}^2$:

$$\boxed{|x_i - x'_j| + |y_i - y'_j| = \max_{s_1, s_2 \in \{-1, +1\}} \Big[ \underbrace{(s_1 x_i + s_2 y_i)}_{\text{Depends ONLY on Red } i} + \underbrace{(-s_1 x'_j - s_2 y'_j)}_{\text{Depends ONLY on Blue } j} \Big].}$$

Look at the right-hand side: for each fixed sign pair $(s_1, s_2) \in \{ (+1, +1), (+1, -1), (-1, +1), (-1, -1) \}$, the interaction between Red pile $i$ and Blue pile $j$ **decouples completely into a sum of a Red-only weight and a Blue-only weight**!

#### Step 3 — Mechanical Graph Compilation Through the 4 Global Sign Hubs $H_{\pm, \pm}$

Introduce **4 global intermediate hub vertices** $\mathcal{H} = \{H_{++}, H_{+-}, H_{-+}, H_{--}\}$ corresponding to the $4$ sign pairs $(s_1, s_2) \in \{-1, +1\}^2$. To convert maximization into standard Min-Cost Max-Flow, we negate all edge costs:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    S(["Source S"]) -->|"cap c_i, cost 0"| Ri["Red Pile R_i"]
    Ri -->|"cap inf, cost -(x_i + y_i)"| Hpp["Hub H_{++}"]
    Ri -->|"cap inf, cost -(x_i - y_i)"| Hpm["Hub H_{+-}"]
    Ri -->|"cap inf, cost -(-x_i + y_i)"| Hmp["Hub H_{-+}"]
    Ri -->|"cap inf, cost -(-x_i - y_i)"| Hmm["Hub H_{--}"]
    Hpp -->|"cap inf, cost +(x'_j + y'_j)"| Bj["Blue Pile B_j"]
    Hpm -->|"cap inf, cost +(x'_j - y'_j)"| Bj
    Hmp -->|"cap inf, cost +(-x'_j + y'_j)"| Bj
    Hmm -->|"cap inf, cost +(-x'_j - y'_j)"| Bj
    Bj -->|"cap d_j, cost 0"| T(["Sink T"])
```

- **Graph Sparsification**:
  - Total vertices: $|V| = 2N + 6 \le 2,006$.
  - Total directed edges: $N$ (`S -> R_i`) $+ 4N$ (`R_i -> H`) $+ 4N$ (`H -> B_j`) $+ N$ (`B_j -> T`) $= 10N \le 10,000$ edges—a **$100\times$ reduction** from $N^2 = 10^6$!
- **Why Different Pairs Sharing a Hub Never Interfere**:
  Because the cost of routing $1$ unit along $R_i \to H_{s_1, s_2} \to B_j$ is strictly additive, any flow entering $H_{s_1, s_2}$ from multiple Red piles and exiting to multiple Blue piles pays the exact sum of their individual linear coordinates regardless of how the units are paired inside $H_{s_1, s_2}$. And because we minimize total negated cost, any unit routed from $R_i$ to $B_j$ will automatically pick the hub $H_{s_1^*, s_2^*}$ that minimizes $-(s_1(x_i - x'_j) + s_2(y_i - y'_j)) = -(|x_i - x'_j| + |y_i - y'_j|)$!
- **$O(N)$ DAG Potential Initialization**:
  Before the first augmentation, the network $S \to R_i \to H_{s_1,s_2} \to B_j \to T$ is a **4-layer DAG**. We compute initial Johnson potentials $\pi(v)$ in $O(N)$ time by a single forward pass:
  $$\pi(S) = \pi(R_i) = 0, \qquad \pi(H_{s_1, s_2}) = \min_{1 \le i \le N} \big(-(s_1 x_i + s_2 y_i)\big), \qquad \pi(B_j) = \min_{s_1, s_2 \in \{\pm 1\}} \big(\pi(H_{s_1, s_2}) + s_1 x'_j + s_2 y'_j\big), \qquad \pi(T) = \min_{1 \le j \le N} \pi(B_j).$$
  This allows every augmentation to run via pure **$O(N \log N)$ Dijkstra** with zero SPFA passes!

::: {.callout-tip title="High-Dimensional Generalization: $2^d$ Hubs for $\ell_1^d$ Manhattan vs. $2d$ Hubs for $\ell_\infty^d$ Chebyshev"}
What if the points lie in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d \ge 3$)?
1. **Manhattan Norm ($\ell_1^d$)**: $\sum_{k=1}^d |p_k - q_k| = \max_{\sigma \in \{\pm 1\}^d} \big(\langle \sigma, p \rangle + \langle -\sigma, q \rangle\big)$ requires **$2^d$ sign hubs** $H_\sigma$.
2. **Chebyshev Norm ($\ell_\infty^d$)**: $\max_{1 \le k \le d} |p_k - q_k| = \max_{1 \le k \le d,\; s \in \{\pm 1\}} \big(s \cdot p_k + (-s \cdot q_k)\big)$ requires **only $2d$ signed-axis hubs** $H_{k, s}$! (In $d = 2$, $2^2 = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$ because $\ell_1^2$ and $\ell_\infty^2$ are $45^\circ$ rotations of each other.)
:::

#### Step 4 — Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Why Sign Hubs Fail for Minimization (`FM-20c`)

- **Numerical Toy Trace ($N = 1$, $R_1 = (1, 5)$, $B_1 = (4, 1)$)**:
  - True Manhattan distance: $|1 - 4| + |5 - 1| = 3 + 4 = 7$.
  - Let us check the negated cost of routing $1$ unit from $R_1(1, 5)$ to $B_1(4, 1)$ through each of the $4$ hubs:
    - $H_{++}$: $-(1 + 5) + (4 + 1) = -6 + 5 = -1$.
    - $H_{+-}$: $-(1 - 5) + (4 - 1) = +4 + 3 = +7$.
    - $H_{-+}$: $-(-1 + 5) + (-4 + 1) = -4 - 3 = -7$ (**Minimum negated cost = $-7 \implies$ Max distance $+7$!**).
    - $H_{--}$: $-(-1 - 5) + (-4 - 1) = +6 - 5 = +1$.
- **Broken-Gadget Counterexample `FM-20c`: Why Sign Hubs Fail Catastrophically for MIN-Cost Manhattan Matching**:
  Suppose a problem asks to **minimize** $\sum (|x_i - x'_j| + |y_i - y'_j|)$ instead of maximizing it, and a contestant builds the exact same 4-hub network without negating costs (so $R_1 \to H_{s_1,s_2} \to B_1$ has cost $s_1(x_1 - x'_1) + s_2(y_1 - y'_1)$).
  - In our toy trace above, what is the minimum cost over the 4 hubs? It is **not** $+7$; the min-cost flow solver picks $H_{-+}$ of cost **$-7 = -\big(|x_1 - x'_1| + |y_1 - y'_1|\big)$**!
  - **Why it broke**: Because $\min_{s_1, s_2 \in \{\pm 1\}} \big(s_1 \Delta x + s_2 \Delta y\big) = -|\Delta x| - |\Delta y|$. A hub layer computes the **minimum** cost among parallel paths $h \in \mathcal{H}$, which can represent a **pointwise maximum** when negated ($\min_h (-f_h) = -\max_h f_h$), but can **never** represent minimizing a pointwise maximum $\min \max_h f_h$!

---

## 6. Worked Examples & Progressive 8-Problem Difficulty Ladder (`#153`–`#160`)

We now apply our five structural modules across the eight canonical contest problems of Chapter 20, progressing from Stepping Stones to Grandmaster Mastery.

### 6.1 Problem `#153` (`SS-1`) — [Luogu P3171 / TJOI2013] 循环格 (Cyclic Torus Grid)

- **Judge URL**: [https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3171](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3171)
- **Bounds**: $R, C \le 15$ ($N = R \times C \le 225$).

#### Problem Statement

Given an $R \times C$ grid on a torus (wrapping top-to-bottom and left-to-right) where each cell $(r, c)$ contains a direction arrow $d_{r,c} \in \{\text{'U'}, \text{'D'}, \text{'L'}, \text{'R'}\}$, find the minimum number of cells whose arrows must be changed so that every cell in the grid has **in-degree $1$ and out-degree $1$** (forming a vertex-disjoint directed cycle cover of the torus).

#### 4-Step Compilation Summary

1. **Step 1 (Diagnostic Signal)**: Each cell has out-degree $1$, and we require every cell to also have in-degree $1$ — i.e., the transition map $(r, c) \mapsto \text{next}(r, c)$ must be a bijection on the $R \times C$ cells. Because $R, C \le 15$, $V = 2RC + 2 \le 452$ is tiny, and we want a minimum-cost permutation of grid cells where edges to the 4 torus neighbors cost $0$ (if matching $d_{r,c}$) or $1$ (if modified).
2. **Step 2 (Algebraic Formulation)**: Let $x_{u, v} \in \{0, 1\}$ for adjacent torus cells $u, v$. Minimize $\sum_{u} \sum_{v \in N(u)} \mathbf{1}[v \neq \text{dir}(u)] x_{u, v}$ subject to $\sum_v x_{u, v} = 1$ (out-degree $1$) and $\sum_u x_{u, v} = 1$ (in-degree $1$).
3. **Step 3 (Graph Compilation)**: Split each cell $u$ into $u_{\text{out}}$ (left) and $u_{\text{in}}$ (right).
   - $S \to u_{\text{out}}$ with $(\text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = 0)$ and $u_{\text{in}} \to T$ with $(\text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = 0)$.
   - For each of the 4 torus neighbors $v$ of $u$, add $u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}$ with $\text{cap} = 1$ and $\text{cost} = 0$ if $v$ lies in direction $d_u$, or $\text{cost} = 1$ otherwise.
4. **Step 4 (Bonus Efficiency Insight)**: Because all edge costs are in $\{0, 1\}$ and all capacities are $1$, any shortest augmenting path step in the residual network has edge weights in $\{-1, 0, +1\}$, and with Johnson potentials all reduced costs are non-negative integers with path length $\le RC$. Standard SSP runs in $< 5\text{ ms}$ for $RC \le 225$.

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Structural Recognition (Problem #153)"}
What does "every cell is visited in a cycle cover, and each cell steps to the next cell along its arrow" mean for the in-degree and out-degree of every cell $(r, c)$?
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Bipartite Split Formulation (Problem #153)"}
Every cell always has out-degree $1$ (it points somewhere). For the arrows to partition the grid into disjoint cycles, every cell must also have **in-degree $1$**. How do we model $\text{out-deg}(u) = 1$ and $\text{in-deg}(v) = 1$ simultaneously as a bipartite assignment?
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Full Network Specification (Problem #153)"}
Split each cell $u = (r, c)$ into $u_{\text{out}}$ and $u_{\text{in}}$. Connect $S \to u_{\text{out}}$ $(1, 0)$ and $u_{\text{in}} \to T$ $(1, 0)$. For each of the 4 torus neighbors $v$ of $u$, add edge $u_{\text{out}} \to v_{\text{in}}$ with capacity $1$ and cost $0$ if $v$ matches $u$'s original arrow, or cost $1$ otherwise. The min-cost max-flow of value $RC$ is the answer.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete C++ Solution — Problem #153 ([TJOI2013] 循环格)"}
```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct MCMF {
    struct Edge { int to, rev, cap, cost; };
    int n;
    vector<vector<Edge>> g;
    vector<int> dist, pv, pe;
    vector<bool> inq;

    MCMF(int n) : n(n), g(n), dist(n), pv(n), pe(n), inq(n) {}

    void add_edge(int u, int v, int cap, int cost) {
        g[u].push_back({v, (int)g[v].size(), cap, cost});
        g[v].push_back({u, (int)g[u].size() - 1, 0, -cost});
    }

    int min_cost_max_flow(int s, int t) {
        int total_cost = 0;
        const int INF = 1e9;
        while (true) {
            fill(dist.begin(), dist.end(), INF);
            fill(inq.begin(), inq.end(), false);
            queue<int> q;
            dist[s] = 0;
            q.push(s);
            inq[s] = true;
            while (!q.empty()) {
                int u = q.front();
                q.pop();
                inq[u] = false;
                for (int i = 0; i < (int)g[u].size(); ++i) {
                    auto &e = g[u][i];
                    if (e.cap > 0 && dist[u] + e.cost < dist[e.to]) {
                        dist[e.to] = dist[u] + e.cost;
                        pv[e.to] = u;
                        pe[e.to] = i;
                        if (!inq[e.to]) {
                            inq[e.to] = true;
                            q.push(e.to);
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            if (dist[t] == INF) break;
            int push = INF;
            for (int v = t; v != s; v = pv[v])
                push = min(push, g[pv[v]][pe[v]].cap);
            for (int v = t; v != s; v = pv[v]) {
                auto &e = g[pv[v]][pe[v]];
                e.cap -= push;
                g[v][e.rev].cap += push;
            }
            total_cost += push * dist[t];
        }
        return total_cost;
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int R, C;
    if (!(cin >> R >> C)) return 0;
    vector<string> grid(R);
    for (int r = 0; r < R; ++r) cin >> grid[r];

    int N = R * C;
    int S = 2 * N, T = 2 * N + 1;
    MCMF mcmf(2 * N + 2);

    const int dr[4] = {-1, 1, 0, 0};
    const int dc[4] = {0, 0, -1, 1};
    const char dir_ch[4] = {'U', 'D', 'L', 'R'};

    for (int r = 0; r < R; ++r) {
        for (int c = 0; c < C; ++c) {
            int u = r * C + c;
            mcmf.add_edge(S, u, 1, 0);
            mcmf.add_edge(N + u, T, 1, 0);
            for (int d = 0; d < 4; ++d) {
                int nr = (r + dr[d] + R) % R;
                int nc = (c + dc[d] + C) % C;
                int v = nr * C + nc;
                int cost = (grid[r][c] == dir_ch[d]) ? 0 : 1;
                mcmf.add_edge(u, N + v, 1, cost);
            }
        }
    }

    cout << mcmf.min_cost_max_flow(S, T) << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```

### 6.2 Problem `#154` (`SS-2`) — [Luogu P2053 / SCOI2007] 修车 (Car Repair)

- **Judge URL**: [https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2053](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2053)
- **Bounds**: $M \le 9$ technicians, $N \le 60$ cars, repair times $t_{i, j} \le 1000$.

#### Problem Statement

$N$ customers bring their cars to a repair shop with $M$ technicians. Technician $j$ takes $t_{i, j}$ minutes to repair car $i$. Each technician repairs their assigned cars sequentially one at a time. Minimize the **average waiting + repair completion time** across all $N$ customers (accurate to $2$ decimal places).

#### 4-Step Compilation Summary

1. **Step 1 (Diagnostic Signal)**: Minimizing $\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N C_i$ is equivalent to minimizing total completion time $\sum_{i=1}^N C_i$. A forward queue index $q$ depends on the durations of the $q - 1$ cars before it (coupled state!), whereas a **reverse queue index** $r \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ (counting from the **last** car repaired by technician $j$) delays exactly $r$ cars (itself plus the $r - 1$ cars after it).
2. **Step 2 (Algebraic Formulation)**: By Equation (2), placing car $i$ into reverse slot $(j, r)$ contributes exactly $r \cdot t_{i, j}$ to $\sum C_i$. Let $x_{i, j, r} \in \{0, 1\}$. Minimize $\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^M \sum_{r=1}^N (r \cdot t_{i, j}) x_{i, j, r}$ subject to $\sum_{j, r} x_{i, j, r} = 1$ for each car $i$, and $\sum_i x_{i, j, r} \le 1$ for each slot $(j, r)$.
3. **Step 3 (Graph Compilation)**:
   - Left nodes: $N$ cars $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, with $S \to i$ $(\text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = 0)$.
   - Right nodes: $M \cdot N$ reverse slots $(j, r)$, with $(j, r) \to T$ $(\text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = 0)$.
   - Bipartite edges: $i \to (j, r)$ with $\text{cap} = 1, \text{cost} = r \cdot t_{i, j}$.
4. **Step 4 (Scale Verification)**: With $N \le 60, M \le 9$, $M \cdot N \le 540$ slots and $N \cdot M \cdot N \le 32{,}400$ edges fit easily in static memory without needing lazy node spawning (which we will deploy in `#156`).

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Breaking Forward-Queue Coupling (Problem #154)"}
If car $i$ is the $q$-th car repaired by technician $j$, its completion time depends on the repair times of the $q - 1$ cars before it. What if instead you count its position $r \in \{1, \dots, k_j\}$ **from the back of technician $j$'s queue** ($r = 1$ is the last car repaired)?
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Contribution Counting (Problem #154)"}
If car $i$ is the $r$-th from last car repaired by technician $j$, how many cars in technician $j$'s queue have to wait for car $i$'s repair to finish? Exactly $r$ cars (car $i$ itself, plus the $r - 1$ cars behind it)! So car $i$'s standalone contribution to the total waiting time is $r \cdot t_{i, j}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Bipartite Assignment Graph (Problem #154)"}
Create $N$ car vertices on the left and $M \times N$ slot vertices $(j, r)$ on the right ($1 \le j \le M, 1 \le r \le N$). Connect car $i$ to slot $(j, r)$ with capacity $1$ and cost $r \cdot t_{i, j}$. Run MCMF and divide the minimum cost by $N$.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Complete C++ Solution — Problem #154 ([SCOI2007] 修车)"}
```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

struct MCMF {
    struct Edge { int to, rev, cap; long long cost; };
    int n;
    vector<vector<Edge>> g;
    vector<long long> dist;
    vector<int> pv, pe;
    vector<bool> inq;

    MCMF(int n) : n(n), g(n), dist(n), pv(n), pe(n), inq(n) {}

    void add_edge(int u, int v, int cap, long long cost) {
        g[u].push_back({v, (int)g[v].size(), cap, cost});
        g[v].push_back({u, (int)g[u].size() - 1, 0, -cost});
    }

    long long min_cost_max_flow(int s, int t) {
        long long total_cost = 0;
        const long long INF = 1e18;
        while (true) {
            fill(dist.begin(), dist.end(), INF);
            fill(inq.begin(), inq.end(), false);
            queue<int> q;
            dist[s] = 0;
            q.push(s);
            inq[s] = true;
            while (!q.empty()) {
                int u = q.front();
                q.pop();
                inq[u] = false;
                for (int i = 0; i < (int)g[u].size(); ++i) {
                    auto &e = g[u][i];
                    if (e.cap > 0 && dist[u] + e.cost < dist[e.to]) {
                        dist[e.to] = dist[u] + e.cost;
                        pv[e.to] = u;
                        pe[e.to] = i;
                        if (!inq[e.to]) {
                            inq[e.to] = true;
                            q.push(e.to);
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            if (dist[t] == INF) break;
            int push = 1e9;
            for (int v = t; v != s; v = pv[v])
                push = min(push, g[pv[v]][pe[v]].cap);
            for (int v = t; v != s; v = pv[v]) {
                auto &e = g[pv[v]][pe[v]];
                e.cap -= push;
                g[v][e.rev].cap += push;
            }
            total_cost += 1LL * push * dist[t];
        }
        return total_cost;
    }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int M, N;
    if (!(cin >> M >> N)) return 0;
    vector<vector<int>> t(N, vector<int>(M));
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < M; ++j)
            cin >> t[i][j];

    int S = N + M * N, T = S + 1;
    MCMF mcmf(T + 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        mcmf.add_edge(S, i, 1, 0);
        for (int j = 0; j < M; ++j) {
            for (int r = 1; r <= N; ++r) {
                int slot = N + j * N + (r - 1);
                mcmf.add_edge(i, slot, 1, 1LL * r * t[i][j]);
            }
        }
    }
    for (int j = 0; j < M; ++j)
        for (int r = 1; r <= N; ++r)
            mcmf.add_edge(N + j * N + (r - 1), T, 1, 0);

    long long min_cost = mcmf.min_cost_max_flow(S, T);
    cout << fixed << setprecision(2) << (double)min_cost / N << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```
